```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>",
                      fig.width = 6, fig.height = 3.5, out.width = "100%")
# A number written for the text: plain for moderate sizes, and as
# m x 10^e (HTML) otherwise
fmt_num <- function(x, digits = 2) {
  x <- signif(x, digits)
  if (!is.finite(x)) return(as.character(x))
  if (abs(x) < 1e-300) return("0")
  e <- floor(log10(abs(x)))
  if (e >= -3 && e <= 4) return(format(x, digits = digits, big.mark = ","))
  sprintf("%s &times; 10<sup>%d</sup>", format(x / 10^e, digits = digits),
          as.integer(e))
}
```

```{r setup}
library(onestepcox)
library(ggplot2)
```

A one-step correction converges to the Cox limit only if its anchor does.
Under proportional hazards, the Mantel-Haenszel estimator converges to the
true log hazard ratio, whereas the Pike and Peto estimators converge to other
values unless the hazard ratio is 1. `LimitHR()` computes these limits under
the design of `GenSimData()`; this article uses it to show how large the
differences are and how they carry over to the one-step corrections.

## Limits over a range of hazard ratios

The design below has equal groups, uniform accrual over a period of length
`a`, and the analysis when a fraction `E / (n_T + n_C)` of the subjects have
had an event. The limits depend on the allocation, the hazards, `a`, and this
fraction, not on the sample size itself.

```{r grid}
design <- list(hazard_C = log(2) / 18, n_T = 100, n_C = 100, a = 12,
               E = 150)
hr <- exp(seq(log(0.1), log(10), length.out = 20))
lim <- do.call(LimitHR, c(list(HR = hr), design))
```

The first figure shows the absolute bias of the estimators whose limits
differ from the true value: the Pike and Peto estimators and the corrections
from the Pike anchor.

```{r figure-abs, fig.alt = "Absolute large-sample bias of the Pike and Peto estimators and of the Newton, Chebyshev, and Halley steps from the Pike estimate against the hazard ratio, on logarithmic scales."}
plot(lim)
```

The second figure shows the signed bias of the anchors and of the Halley
steps from each anchor. The Mantel-Haenszel anchor and the MH-Halley
estimator stay on the line at zero.

```{r figure-signed, fig.alt = "Signed large-sample bias of the Mantel-Haenszel, Pike, and Peto estimators and of the Halley steps from the Mantel-Haenszel and Pike estimates against the hazard ratio."}
plot(lim, methods = c("MH", "MH_Halley", "Pike", "Pike_Halley", "Peto"),
     scale = "signed")
```

## The bias at selected hazard ratios

```{r table}
hr_tab <- c(0.2, 0.5, 2, 5, 10)
lim_tab <- as.data.frame(do.call(LimitHR, c(list(HR = hr_tab), design)))
shown <- c("Pike", "Peto", "Pike_Newton", "Pike_Halley", "MH", "MH_Halley")
tiny <- 1e-12
fmt_bias <- function(x) if (abs(x) < tiny) "0" else fmt_num(x)
tab <- sapply(hr_tab, function(h) {
  vapply(shown, function(m) {
    fmt_bias(lim_tab$bias[lim_tab$method == m & abs(lim_tab$HR - h) < 1e-8])
  }, character(1))
})
colnames(tab) <- paste("HR", hr_tab)
rownames(tab) <- gsub("_", "-", shown)
knitr::kable(tab, align = "rrrrr",
             caption = "Large-sample bias of the log hazard ratio")
```

Values smaller than `r fmt_num(tiny)` in absolute value, which are rounding
error, are shown as 0.

```{r table-numbers, include = FALSE}
bias_at <- function(m, h) {
  lim_tab$bias[lim_tab$method == m & abs(lim_tab$HR - h) < 1e-8]
}
h_max <- max(hr_tab)
```

At a hazard ratio of `r h_max`, the limit of the Pike estimator differs from
the true value by `r fmt_num(abs(bias_at("Pike", h_max)))` on the log
scale. One Newton step
from it leaves `r fmt_num(abs(bias_at("Pike_Newton", h_max)))`, and one
Halley step `r fmt_num(abs(bias_at("Pike_Halley", h_max)))`, which no longer
shrinks as the sample size grows. The MH-Halley limit is the true value up
to rounding error.

## Finite samples approach the limits

In simulated trials of this design with increasing sample sizes, the mean
difference between each estimate and the Cox estimate approaches the
difference between their limits. Because the Cox estimator converges to the
true value, that difference is the large-sample bias of the estimator.

```{r finite}
hr_check <- 5
sizes <- c(200, 1000, 5000)
frac <- design$E / (design$n_T + design$n_C)
check_sc <- data.frame(label = paste("n =", sizes), n_T = sizes / 2,
                       n_C = sizes / 2, hazard_C = design$hazard_C,
                       HR = hr_check, a = design$a, E = frac * sizes)
fin <- CompareOC(check_sc,
                 methods = c("Cox_NR", "Pike", "Pike_Halley", "MH",
                             "MH_Halley"),
                 nsim = 50, seed = 1, reference = "Cox_NR")
est <- fin$estimates
ref <- est[est$method == "Cox_NR", c("label", "simID", "coef")]
names(ref)[3] <- "coef_ref"
dev <- merge(est[est$method != "Cox_NR", ], ref, by = c("label", "simID"))
dev$d <- dev$coef - dev$coef_ref
mean_dev <- aggregate(d ~ label + method, data = dev, FUN = mean)
mean_dev$n <- sizes[match(as.character(mean_dev$label), check_sc$label)]
lim_check <- as.data.frame(do.call(LimitHR, c(list(HR = hr_check), design)))
mean_dev$limit <- lim_check$bias[match(mean_dev$method, lim_check$method)]
```

```{r finite-numbers, include = FALSE}
at <- function(m) {
  x <- mean_dev[mean_dev$method == m, ]
  x[which.max(x$n), ]
}
```

Each panel has its own vertical scale; the dashed lines are the large-sample
biases.

```{r figure-finite, fig.height = 4.5, fig.alt = "Mean difference from the Cox_NR estimate against the sample size, in one panel for each of the Pike and Mantel-Haenszel estimators and the Halley steps from them, with dashed lines at the large-sample bias."}
plot_d <- mean_dev
plot_d$method <- gsub("_", "-", plot_d$method)
ggplot(plot_d, aes(x = n, y = d)) +
  geom_hline(aes(yintercept = limit), linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  geom_line() +
  scale_x_log10() +
  facet_wrap(~ method, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = "Number of subjects",
       y = "Mean difference from Cox-NR (log HR)") +
  theme_bw()
```

With a hazard ratio of `r hr_check`, `r fmt_num(max(sizes))` subjects, and
`r attr(fin, "nsim")` trials, the mean difference of the Pike estimator from
the Cox estimate is
`r fmt_num(at("Pike")$d)`, compared with a large-sample bias of
`r fmt_num(at("Pike")$limit)`, and that of one Halley step from the Pike
estimate is `r fmt_num(at("Pike_Halley")$d)`, compared with
`r fmt_num(at("Pike_Halley")$limit)`. The mean differences of the
Mantel-Haenszel estimator and of MH-Halley, whose limits are the true value,
are `r fmt_num(at("MH")$d)` and `r fmt_num(at("MH_Halley")$d)`.
